name: Logstash
license: Apache 2.0 (core and plugins); `x-pack` code under the Elastic License, included in the default download but not in the `-oss` builds
summary: Elastic’s JVM-based pipeline that takes events in, parses them with filters such as `grok`, and sends them on, most often to Elasticsearch.
intro: Logstash is a server process that runs pipelines of three stages. Inputs receive events (from Beats and Elastic Agent, files, syslog, Kafka, S3 or a scheduled SQL query), filters parse and enrich them, and outputs send them on, most often to Elasticsearch. The best-known filter is `grok`, which turns an unstructured log line into named fields using about 120 built-in regular-expression patterns. Worker threads, one per CPU core by default, take events from a queue in batches of 125 and run them through the filters and outputs. That queue lives in memory unless you switch on the persistent queue, which writes events to disk (up to 1 GB by default) so they survive a restart; it is not replicated, so it does not survive losing the disk.

Logstash runs on the JVM: its core is Java and JRuby, plugins are Ruby gems (over 200 of them), and the downloads bundle a Temurin 21 JDK. It is free to use. The repository mixes licences: code outside the `x-pack` folder is Apache 2.0, code inside it is under the Elastic License, and the default download contains both; builds with `-oss` in the name contain only the Apache 2.0 parts. Elastic’s 2021 move of Elasticsearch and Kibana to SSPL and the Elastic License, and the AGPL option it added for them in 2024, did not apply to Logstash. Some features, such as managing pipelines centrally from Kibana, need a paid Elastic subscription.
strengths: Flexible parsing in one readable config: `grok`, `date`, `mutate`, `drop`, `clone` and `geoip` filters, with conditionals between them
The natural fit for Elasticsearch and Kibana; the `beats` input, and its successor `elastic_agent`, receive data from Elastic’s own shippers
Over 200 plugins, including Kafka, S3, JDBC and Redis, each a separate gem that is released on its own
The persistent queue gives at-least-once delivery through restarts and crashes, for inputs that acknowledge what they receive
The core stayed Apache 2.0 through all of Elastic’s licence changes
limits: Heavy for running on every host: a JVM for which Elastic recommends a 4 to 8 GB heap in typical ingestion setups
The default memory queue loses in-flight events if the machine fails; the persistent queue is off by default, cannot protect inputs without acknowledgements (TCP, UDP), and is not replicated
Mixed licensing to keep track of: the default download includes Elastic License code, the `-oss` build drops every `x-pack` feature, and centralized pipeline management needs a subscription
Grok patterns are regular expressions, so parsing a new log format means writing and testing patterns by hand

sections.title: Which parts are open source
sections.intro: Logstash is often lumped in with Elasticsearch’s licence changes. The repository’s `LICENSE.txt` says what applies today.

items.name: Core and plugins
items.text: Every file outside the `x-pack` folder is Apache 2.0 unless it says otherwise. Plugins live in their own repositories under `logstash-plugins` and ship as Ruby gems.

items.name: The `x-pack` folder
items.text: Elastic’s extra features, such as monitoring, central pipeline management and GeoIP database management, merged into the repository in April 2018. Their source is readable, but under the Elastic License, not an open-source licence.

items.name: Default download
items.text: Contains the Apache 2.0 code and the `x-pack` code. Free features are on by default; subscription features, such as centralized pipeline management, need a paid licence or a 30-day trial.

items.name: `-oss` download
items.text: Elastic still publishes these builds (9.5.4 in September 2026). They include only Apache 2.0 features.

items.name: 2021 and 2024
items.text: In January 2021 Elasticsearch and Kibana moved from Apache 2.0 to SSPL and the Elastic License, and in 2024 Elastic added AGPL as a third option for them. Elastic’s licensing FAQ says the changes covered only Elasticsearch and Kibana, and that Logstash and Beats remain Apache 2.0.

story: Jordan Sissel, who had worked at Google, Loggly and Heroku, started Logstash as an open-source project in 2009; the first prototype commit, by Pete Fritchman, is from August that year. The idea was a generic event processor: a log could be any timestamped piece of data, and inputs, filters and outputs could be combined freely. It was written in Ruby, with a short text config in three stages that made it easy to move data from any source to any destination.

Sissel says he designed Logstash from day one to work with Elasticsearch and Kibana, and the three became known as the ELK stack. In August 2013 he joined Elasticsearch, the company, which began selling support for Logstash the same day, alongside the release of Logstash 1.2.

JRuby became Logstash’s usual runtime for speed and for Java libraries, but crossing between Ruby and Java cost CPU and memory, so Elastic moved the internals to Java. A Java execution engine, previewed in 6.3 in 2018, became the default in 7.0 in 2019. When Elasticsearch and Kibana left Apache 2.0 in 2021, Logstash’s core stayed.

choices.why: Sissel wanted a generic system where any input, processing step and output could be composed. The simple model and text config proved a friendly way to get data from point A to point B.
Sissel says he designed it from day one to work with Elasticsearch and Kibana: Logstash pulls events off systems, Elasticsearch stores and searches them, and Kibana charts the results.

choices.choice: Run on JRuby, then move the core to Java
choices.why: JRuby gave Ruby code the JVM’s speed and its libraries. As more plugins were written in Java, compiling pipelines to JVM bytecode removed the cost of crossing between the two languages and cut startup and reload times.
